title: malloc and free
lesson:
So far every array had a size fixed when you wrote the program: `double temps[5]`. But a sensor log might hold 10 readings or 10,000, and you only find out while the program runs. Local arrays also vanish when their function returns. For both problems, C lets you ask for memory from the **heap**: a big pool that lasts until you give it back.

```
#include <stdlib.h>

int n = 500;
double *readings = malloc(n * sizeof *readings);
if (readings == NULL) {
    printf("out of memory\n");
    return 1;
}
readings[0] = 21.5;          /* use it like an array */
...
free(readings);              /* give it back, exactly once */
readings = NULL;             /* so nobody uses it by mistake */
```

- `malloc(bytes)` returns a pointer to a new block, or **NULL** if there isn't enough memory. On a PC that's rare; on a microcontroller with 2 KB it's real. Always check.
- `n * sizeof *readings` asks for n items of whatever `readings` points to. If you later change the type, this stays right.
- The block is **not cleared**: it holds leftover junk until you write to it. (`calloc(n, size)` gives zeroed memory.)
- Every `malloc` needs exactly one `free`. Whoever owns the pointer is responsible for freeing it.

**Three bugs in plain words:**
- **Leak**: you forget to free. The memory stays taken until the program ends. In a program that runs for days (a weather station, a game server), leaks pile up until it crashes.
- **Use-after-free**: you free a block, then read or write it. It may seem to work, then break later in strange ways. Set the pointer to `NULL` after freeing.
- **Double free**: freeing the same block twice. This can corrupt the heap. `free(NULL)` is safe and does nothing, which is another reason to set pointers to `NULL`.

**How Archie checks your memory.** In these exercises your file has three small helpers: `my_alloc`, `my_realloc` and `my_free`. They call the real functions and also count: `live_allocs` goes up on each allocation and down on each free. The tests check that it's back where it started when your code is done, so a leak shows up as a failed test, not a mystery crash next week. Real projects use tools like this too (Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, or a counter in an embedded build).

**The professional habit:** write the `free` at the same time you write the `malloc`, then fill in the code between them.

notes: make_log asks for n doubles with malloc(n * sizeof *log).
It returns NULL when n is 0 or when malloc fails, and main checks for that.
Returning the pointer hands ownership to main: main must free it.
The array outlives make_log, which a local array never could.
free(log) then log = NULL: free once, and make any later mistake obvious.

exercises.title: An array of n readings
exercises.prompt: Write int *make_readings(int n, int start, int step). It allocates an array of n ints with malloc and fills it with start, start + step, start + 2*step, ... The caller frees it. If n is 0 or negative, or malloc fails, return NULL.

tests.call: ({ int *a = make_readings(4, 10, 5); int r = a[0] * 1000 + a[3]; free(a); r; })
tests.name: four readings

tests.call: ({ int *a = make_readings(3, 100, -20); int r = a[2]; free(a); r; })
tests.name: counting down

hints: Check n <= 0 at the top, and a == NULL after malloc.
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = start + i * step;

exercises.title: Copy the log
exercises.prompt: Write double *copy_log(const double *src, int n): a new heap copy of the n readings, made with my_alloc (not malloc), so the caller can change the copy without touching the original. If n is 0 or negative, return NULL without allocating.

tests.call: ({ double a[] = {1.5, 2.5, 4.0}; double *c = copy_log(a, 3); double r = c[0] + c[2]; my_free(c); r; })
tests.name: copies the values

tests.call: ({ double a[] = {1.5}; double *c = copy_log(a, 1); c[0] = 9.0; double r = a[0]; my_free(c); r; })
tests.name: a real copy, not the same memory
tests.hint_if_fail: Allocate a new block and copy into it; don't return src.

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; double a[] = {1, 2, 3}; double *c = copy_log(a, 3); int r = (live_allocs - before) * 100 + (int)(last_alloc_size / sizeof(double)); my_free(c); r; })
tests.name: one block of n doubles

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; double a[] = {1}; double *c = copy_log(a, 0); (c == NULL) * 10 + (live_allocs - before); })
tests.name: n of 0: NULL, nothing allocated

hints: Check copy == NULL, then copy each value in a loop (or memcpy).
memcpy(copy, src, n * sizeof *copy); also works.

exercises.title: Fix the leak
exercises.prompt: int max_smoothed(const int *a, int n) works out the average of each neighbouring pair, (a[i] + a[i+1]) / 2 in whole numbers, into a temporary heap array and returns the biggest. It gives the right answers, but it leaks: every call loses a block. Fix it so it frees what it allocates. With fewer than 2 values it returns 0 and allocates nothing.

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; max_smoothed((int[]){1, 2, 3}, 3); live_allocs - before; })
tests.name: no leak
tests.hint_if_fail: Free the temporary array before returning (save best first).

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) max_smoothed((int[]){5, 7}, 2); live_allocs - before; })
tests.name: no leak over 100 calls

tests.call: ({ int before = live_allocs; int r = max_smoothed((int[]){5}, 1); r * 10 + (live_allocs - before); })
tests.name: one value: 0, nothing allocated

hints: The block s is never given back.
You need best after freeing, so keep it in a variable first.

quiz.q: malloc returns NULL. What does that mean?
choices: There wasn't enough memory; you must not use the pointer

quiz.q: Why write malloc(n * sizeof *p) instead of malloc(n * 8)?
choices: It stays correct for whatever type p points to
quiz.why: The size follows the type automatically.

quiz.q: A program frees a block and later reads from it. This is called...
choices: Fine, if it prints the right thing
quiz.why: Freed memory can be reused for something else at any time.

quiz.q: A logger mallocs a buffer for each reading and never frees it. After running for a week...
choices: Memory use keeps growing until the program fails
C frees it automatically every hour
quiz.why: That's a leak; C has no garbage collector.

quiz.q: Why set p = NULL after free(p)?
choices: Using p afterwards then fails clearly, and free(NULL) is safe if it happens again
quiz.why: A NULL pointer can't silently point at reused memory.

cards.a: double *p = malloc(n * sizeof *p); then check p != NULL.
Exactly once for every successful malloc, by whoever owns it.
Allocated memory that is never freed.

explain: Explain the difference between a leak and a use-after-free in your own words, with a short made-up story about a program that has each.
